items.stem: Why must at least one backup copy be offline or immutable to defend against ransomware?

options.text: So attackers who reach the live systems cannot also delete or encrypt the backups
options.rationale: Correct: offline/immutable copies survive an attack that destroys online backups.

options.text: Because offline backups restore faster than any other
options.rationale: Resilience, not speed, is the reason.

options.text: Because immutable backups need no testing
Because online backups cannot be reached by ransomware
options.rationale: Online, writable backups can be encrypted or deleted.

items.explanation: Correct: offline/immutable copies survive an attack that destroys online backups.

items.stem: Which TWO controls help limit how far ransomware spreads once inside a network? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Least-privilege access for users and admins
options.rationale: Correct: limited privileges reduce what malware can reach.

options.text: Giving every user local administrator rights
options.rationale: Broad admin rights help ransomware spread.

options.text: Disabling all logging during an incident
options.rationale: Disabling logging blinds responders and aids the attacker.

items.stem: Why is paying a ransom an unreliable recovery strategy?

options.text: Payment does not guarantee working decryption or that data was not copied
options.rationale: Correct: decryption may fail and data may already be stolen.

options.text: Payment always restores all data perfectly
options.rationale: Recovery after payment is frequently incomplete.

options.text: Paying removes the attacker from the network
options.rationale: Payment does not evict the attacker or close the entry point.
Paying can mark an organisation as a willing target.

items.explanation: Correct: decryption may fail and data may already be stolen.
